courses.summary: Learn what Python is, how analysts use it on tables of data, and how short scripts automate repetitive work.

lessons.title: What Python is
lessons.why: Python is one of the most widely used languages for data, automation and AI work, and it is often the first language people learn.
lessons.try: Open a free online notebook (for example on Kaggle) and run print("Hello, Path.AI").

lessons.title: Working with tables of data
lessons.why: Most office data lives in tables. pandas lets you filter, group and summarise thousands of rows with a few lines of code — work that can take hours by hand.
lessons.try: Load a small CSV file with pandas.read_csv() and show its first five rows with .head().

lessons.title: Automating everyday tasks
lessons.why: A short script can rename files, merge reports or send reminders automatically, freeing your time for work that needs judgement.
lessons.try: Pick one task you repeat every week and write down, step by step, what a script would need to do.

quiz.q: Which feature does Python emphasise?
options: Programs written only in machine code
quiz.explain: Python emphasises readability, simplicity and significant indentation.

quiz.q: Who began working on Python in the late 1980s?
quiz.explain: Guido van Rossum started Python as a successor to the ABC language.

quiz.q: What is the pandas library mainly used for?
options: Data manipulation and analysis of tables and time series
quiz.explain: pandas offers data structures and operations for numerical tables and time series.

quiz.q: Which library is pandas built upon?
quiz.explain: The lesson notes that pandas is built upon NumPy.

quiz.q: What is a script?
options: A short, simple set of instructions that automates an otherwise manual process
quiz.explain: Scripts are short instruction sets that automate manual processes.

courses.summary: Understand relational databases, ask questions of data with SQL, and combine tables with joins.

lessons.title: Relational databases
lessons.why: Customer lists, sales and HR records in most organisations sit in relational databases. Knowing how they are organised helps you find the data you need.
lessons.try: Sketch two tables you use at work (for example Customers and Orders) and mark the column that links them.

lessons.title: Asking questions with SQL
lessons.why: SQL lets you pull exactly the rows you need from millions of records with one query, instead of filtering spreadsheets by hand.
lessons.try: In a free online SQL playground, run SELECT * on a sample table, then add a WHERE condition to filter it.

lessons.title: Combining tables with joins
lessons.why: Real business questions span several tables — for example matching orders to customers. Joins are how you answer them.
lessons.try: Describe in plain words which rows an INNER JOIN of Customers and Orders on customer ID would return.

quiz.q: A relational database stores data in a structured format using…
quiz.explain: An RDBMS stores data in rows and columns.

quiz.q: Who proposed the relational model of data in 1970?
quiz.explain: E. F. Codd proposed the relational model in 1970.

quiz.q: What is SQL mainly used for?
options: Managing data, especially in relational database management systems
quiz.explain: SQL is a domain-specific language for managing data, especially in an RDBMS.

quiz.q: Which operations belong to data manipulation in SQL?
quiz.explain: Data manipulation covers insert, update and delete.

quiz.q: What does a JOIN clause do?
options: Combines columns from one or more tables into a new table
quiz.explain: A join stitches tables together, putting records with matching fields on the same row.

courses.summary: Learn the steps of data analysis: inspect, explore and clean data before drawing conclusions.

lessons.title: What data analysis is
lessons.why: Analysis turns raw numbers into decisions. Employers value people who can find the story in data and explain it simply.
lessons.try: Pick a report you received recently and write down the one decision it was meant to support.

lessons.title: Exploring a new dataset
lessons.why: Exploring first — counts, ranges, charts — stops you from building conclusions on data you don't understand.
lessons.try: Open any dataset and note the number of rows, the columns, and the smallest and largest value of one column.

lessons.title: Cleaning messy data
lessons.why: Typos, duplicates and blanks are common in real data. Cleaning them first makes every result more trustworthy.
lessons.try: Find three problems in a spreadsheet you use (duplicates, blank cells, inconsistent spellings) and fix them.

quiz.q: Which best describes data analysis?
options: Inspecting, cleansing, transforming and modelling data to support decisions
quiz.explain: Data analysis inspects, cleanses, transforms and models data to inform decisions.

quiz.q: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) focuses on…
options: discovering new features in the data
quiz.explain: EDA discovers new features; confirmatory analysis tests existing hypotheses.

quiz.q: EDA often summarises a dataset's main characteristics using…
options: statistical graphics and other visualisation methods
quiz.explain: EDA relies on statistical graphics and visualisation.

quiz.q: Who promoted exploratory data analysis from 1970?
quiz.explain: John Tukey promoted EDA to encourage statisticians to explore data.

quiz.q: Data cleansing is the process of…
options: identifying and correcting or removing corrupt, inaccurate or irrelevant records
quiz.explain: Cleansing detects and fixes incomplete, incorrect or inaccurate data.

courses.summary: Turn numbers into clear charts and dashboards that help people make decisions.

lessons.title: Why we visualise data
lessons.why: A clear chart lets a manager see a trend in seconds. Good visuals make your analysis persuasive.
lessons.try: Take one table from a report and decide which chart — bar, line or map — shows its main message best.

lessons.title: Dashboards
lessons.why: Dashboards give teams an at-a-glance view of the numbers they track every day, such as sales or service levels.
lessons.try: List the three to five numbers your team checks most often — that is the start of a dashboard.

lessons.title: Business intelligence
lessons.why: BI connects data to decisions such as pricing, priorities and goals, which is why BI analysts are in demand.
lessons.try: Name one internal and one external data source that together would help your organisation make a better decision.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of data visualisation?
options: Helping an audience quickly understand patterns, trends and outliers
quiz.explain: Visualisation helps people explore and quickly understand structures, trends and outliers.

quiz.q: Visualisations that convey information to the public in an engaging way are typically called…
quiz.explain: The lesson calls these infographics.

quiz.q: A dashboard typically provides…
options: at-a-glance views of data relevant to an objective
quiz.explain: Dashboards combine visualisations and summaries for at-a-glance views.

quiz.q: Where does the term 'dashboard' come from?
options: The car dashboard where drivers monitor major functions at a glance
quiz.explain: The term comes from the automobile dashboard.

quiz.q: According to the lesson, BI is most effective when it combines…
options: external market data with internal company data
quiz.explain: Combining external and internal data creates intelligence no single source provides.

courses.summary: Summarise data with the right numbers — averages and spread — and test ideas with A/B experiments.

lessons.title: Describing data
lessons.why: Before any advanced analysis, you need to summarise data correctly: the average, the range and how spread out the values are.
lessons.try: For a column of numbers you use (sales, response times), find the minimum, maximum and average.

lessons.title: Mean, median and mode
lessons.why: The median is the middle value when numbers are sorted. One very large value can pull the mean up while the median stays put, so choosing the right average matters.
lessons.try: Work out the mean and the median of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 100 and compare them.

lessons.title: Testing ideas with A/B tests
lessons.why: A/B tests let a team try a change — a new email subject or web page — on real users before rolling it out to everyone.
lessons.try: Design a simple A/B test for something at work: what are versions A and B, and how will you measure success?

quiz.q: Descriptive statistics aims to…
quiz.explain: Descriptive statistics summarises a sample rather than inferring about a population.

quiz.q: Which of these is a measure of variability (spread)?
quiz.explain: Standard deviation measures spread; mean, median and mode measure central tendency.

quiz.q: In mathematics, 'average' most commonly refers to…
quiz.explain: The average most commonly means the arithmetic mean.

quiz.q: What is the median of 1, 2, 3, 4 and 100?
quiz.explain: Sorted, the middle value is 3. The mean is 22 because the value 100 pulls it up.

quiz.q: An A/B test is…
quiz.explain: A/B tests are randomised experiments, usually comparing two variants.

courses.summary: Understand how machines learn from data, how supervised learning works, and why overfitting matters.

lessons.title: What machine learning is
lessons.why: Machine learning powers recommendations, fraud detection and forecasting. Knowing its basics helps you work with data scientists and judge AI tools.
lessons.try: Name one prediction your organisation makes (demand, late payments, staff turnover) and the past data that could train a model.

lessons.title: Learning from labelled examples
lessons.why: Most business machine learning is supervised: learning from past examples where the right answer is known, such as which invoices were paid late.
lessons.try: For an email spam filter, write down what the inputs are and what the labels are.

lessons.title: Overfitting
lessons.why: A model that memorises its training data can look perfect in testing yet fail on new cases — a costly mistake in real decisions.
lessons.try: Explain to a colleague, in one sentence, why a student who memorises past exam answers might fail a new exam.

quiz.q: Machine learning algorithms…
options: must be explicitly programmed for every case
learn from data and generalise to unseen data
quiz.explain: ML algorithms learn from data and generalise without being explicitly programmed.

quiz.q: Advances in deep learning allowed which class of algorithms to surpass many earlier approaches?
quiz.explain: Deep learning let neural networks outperform many earlier ML methods.

quiz.q: Supervised learning trains a model using…
options: labelled data with the correct output for each input
quiz.explain: Each training input comes with the correct output (a label).

quiz.q: Predicting a house price is an example of…
quiz.explain: Regression predicts a numerical value, such as a house price.

quiz.q: Overfitting means a model…
options: fits its training data too closely and fails on new data
is too simple to capture the data's structure
quiz.explain: An overfitted model treats noise as structure. Being too simple is underfitting.

courses.summary: See how large language models work, how RAG grounds them in your documents, and what AI agents can do.

lessons.title: Large language models
lessons.why: LLMs are the engine behind today's AI assistants, and building with them is one of the fastest-rising skills in recent job posts.
lessons.try: Ask an AI assistant to summarise a public report, then check two facts in the summary against the original.

lessons.title: Retrieval-augmented generation
lessons.why: RAG lets an assistant answer from your organisation's own documents — policies, manuals — with sources, instead of guessing.
lessons.try: Pick three internal documents a RAG assistant should search to answer staff questions about leave policy.

lessons.title: AI agents
lessons.why: Agents go beyond chat: they plan multi-step tasks and use tools. Knowing their limits helps you decide what to automate and where people must stay in control.
lessons.try: Write the steps an agent would take to book a meeting room, and mark the step that needs a human to approve.

quiz.q: A large language model is trained on…
quiz.explain: LLMs are trained on vast amounts of text for language tasks.

quiz.q: Most LLMs are based on which neural network architecture?
quiz.explain: LLMs are typically based on the transformer architecture.

quiz.q: What does retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) add to an LLM?
options: Information retrieved from external documents before it answers
quiz.explain: RAG first refers to a specified set of documents, then responds.

quiz.q: One benefit of RAG mentioned in the lesson is that it…
options: removes the need for any data
makes models smaller than a phone app
quiz.explain: Grounding answers in documents helps LLMs stick to the facts.

quiz.q: Which is a common attribute of AI agents?
options: They can perform multi-step tasks and use external tools
They only answer one question at a time
quiz.explain: Agents are goal-directed, use tools and can autonomously perform multi-step tasks.

courses.summary: Use generative AI tools well at work: write clear prompts and check answers for mistakes.

lessons.title: Generative AI at work
lessons.why: Generative AI tools are now used across many jobs. Knowing what they can and cannot do is a basic workplace skill.
lessons.try: Ask an AI assistant to draft a polite email declining a meeting, then edit it into your own voice.

lessons.title: Writing effective prompts
lessons.why: Clear prompts get better answers. Giving the AI a role, an example and the format you want often saves several rounds of edits.
lessons.try: Rewrite a vague prompt ("write about our product") by adding a role, the audience, one example and the output format.

lessons.title: When AI makes things up
lessons.why: AI can state false information confidently. Always check facts, numbers and citations before you use AI output at work.
lessons.try: Ask an AI tool for three sources on a topic and verify that each one really exists.

quiz.q: Generative AI models create new content by…
options: learning patterns and structures from their training data
quiz.explain: They learn underlying patterns in training data and use them to generate new data.

quiz.q: Prompt engineering is…
options: structuring inputs to get specified outputs from a generative AI model
quiz.explain: It is the practice of designing and refining instructions given to a generative model.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common prompting technique?
quiz.explain: Few-shot, chain-of-thought and role assignment are common techniques.

quiz.q: An AI 'hallucination' is…
options: a response containing false or misleading information presented as fact
quiz.explain: Hallucinations are false or misleading statements presented as fact.

quiz.q: Which example of hallucination does the lesson mention?
quiz.explain: LLM chatbots may embed plausible-sounding falsehoods such as fabricated citations.

courses.summary: Learn how teams put machine learning models into production and keep them reliable.

lessons.title: What MLOps is
lessons.why: Most of a model's value appears only after it is deployed and maintained. MLOps skills bridge data science and IT operations.
lessons.try: List what could go wrong after a model goes live: bad input data, slow responses, outdated predictions.

lessons.title: Shipping changes safely
lessons.why: Small, frequent, automated releases make changes less risky — for software and for machine learning models alike.
lessons.try: Write the steps your team follows to release a change and circle the ones that could be automated.

lessons.title: When the world changes: drift
lessons.why: Customer behaviour, prices and regulations change. Monitoring for drift tells you when a model needs retraining.
lessons.try: Think of an event — a holiday season, a new law — that could make last year's data a poor guide for this year.

quiz.q: MLOps aims to…
options: deploy and maintain ML models in production reliably and efficiently
quiz.explain: MLOps bridges ML development and production operations.

quiz.q: The word MLOps combines machine learning with which practice?
quiz.explain: It joins machine learning with DevOps' continuous delivery (CI/CD).

quiz.q: Continuous delivery means…
options: producing software in short cycles so it can be released reliably at any time
quiz.explain: CD keeps software releasable at any time through short cycles.

quiz.q: Continuous delivery helps reduce…
options: the cost, time and risk of delivering changes
quiz.explain: Incremental updates lower the cost, time and risk of change.

quiz.q: Concept drift happens when…
options: the statistical properties of what a model predicts change over time
quiz.explain: Drift makes predictions less accurate as the world changes.

courses.summary: See how data engineers build pipelines that move and clean data, and the warehouses that store it.

lessons.title: What data engineers do
lessons.why: Analysts and AI models depend on reliable data. Data engineers build the systems that collect and prepare it.
lessons.try: Trace one number in a report: which system creates it, how it is moved, and where it is stored.

lessons.title: ETL pipelines
lessons.why: ETL automates the copy-and-paste work of combining data from many systems, such as payroll, sales and purchasing.
lessons.try: For one weekly report, write what is extracted, how it is transformed, and where it is loaded.

lessons.title: Data warehouses
lessons.why: A warehouse gives one trusted place for reporting, so teams stop arguing about whose numbers are right.
lessons.try: List three systems in your organisation whose data you would combine in a warehouse.

quiz.q: Data engineering focuses on…
options: building data systems that enable the collection and use of data
quiz.explain: Data engineering builds the systems that make data usable.

quiz.q: What does ETL stand for?
quiz.explain: ETL = extract, transform, load.

quiz.q: ETL systems commonly…
quiz.explain: ETL typically integrates data from several systems and vendors.

quiz.q: A data warehouse is…
options: a storage room for paper files
a central repository of integrated data used for reporting and analysis
quiz.explain: Warehouses integrate data from disparate sources for reporting and analysis.

quiz.q: Which two workflows are named for building a data warehouse?
quiz.explain: The two main workflows are ETL and ELT.

courses.summary: Learn the main ethical risks of AI — bias, opacity, privacy — and how organisations can govern them.

lessons.title: The ethics of AI
lessons.why: As AI influences hiring, lending and public services, organisations need people who can spot risks and set fair rules.
lessons.try: Pick one AI tool used at your workplace and list who could be harmed if it made a wrong decision.

lessons.title: Bias in algorithms
lessons.why: Biased data can lead to unfair outcomes for groups of people. Checking for bias protects people and the organisation.
lessons.try: Name one way the data used to train a hiring tool could be unrepresentative.

lessons.title: Explaining AI decisions
lessons.why: If people cannot understand why an AI decided something, they cannot challenge or correct it. Explainability builds trust.
lessons.try: Write the explanation a customer should receive if an AI system rejects their application.

quiz.q: Which topic is part of AI ethics?
quiz.explain: AI ethics covers bias, fairness, accountability, transparency, privacy and regulation.

quiz.q: Algorithmic bias describes…
options: systematic tendencies that create unfair outcomes
quiz.explain: It is a systematic, repeatable tendency to create unfair outcomes.

quiz.q: Bias can emerge from…
options: how data is collected, selected or used to train the algorithm
quiz.explain: Data collection, selection and use can all introduce bias.

quiz.q: Which EU law adopted in 2024 is mentioned in the lesson?
quiz.explain: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act was adopted in 2024.

quiz.q: Explainable AI (XAI) aims to…
options: make AI decisions understandable and transparent to people
make AI faster at any cost
quiz.explain: XAI counters the 'black box' so people can oversee AI decisions.

courses.summary: Discover how computers understand images, detect objects, and why CNNs became the standard tool.

lessons.title: What computer vision is
lessons.why: Computer vision is used for factory quality checks, crop monitoring and medical imaging — practical in many industries.
lessons.try: Find one task at work where someone checks images or video by eye. That is a computer-vision opportunity.

lessons.title: Finding objects in images
lessons.why: Detecting and counting objects — people, vehicles, defects — is one of the most practical vision tasks.
lessons.try: List the objects a camera would need to detect to count cars entering a car park.

lessons.title: Convolutional neural networks
lessons.why: CNNs learn useful image features automatically, which is why they became the standard approach for vision tasks.
lessons.try: Explain why reusing one small filter across an image needs far fewer weights than connecting every pixel.

quiz.q: Computer vision is about…
options: acquiring, processing and understanding digital images
quiz.explain: It covers acquiring, processing, analysing and understanding images.

quiz.q: Which is a subdiscipline of computer vision?
quiz.explain: Object detection is listed among computer-vision subdisciplines.

quiz.q: Object detection finds instances of objects of a certain class, such as…
quiz.explain: It detects semantic objects such as humans, buildings or cars.

quiz.q: CNNs are the de facto standard for…
options: deep-learning approaches to computer vision and image processing
quiz.explain: CNNs are standard in deep-learning computer vision.

quiz.q: CNNs learn features through…
options: manual labelling of every pixel by a programmer
quiz.explain: A CNN learns features via filter (kernel) optimisation.
